identity.title: Asymmetric Perturbation in Solving Bilinear Saddle-Point Optimization

problem.claim: Solve bilinear saddle-point optimization problems arising in minimax, game-theoretic, and constrained-optimization settings.

gap.claim: Symmetric perturbation must decrease in strength to converge to an equilibrium of the original game, which leads to a slower rate.

contributions.claim: Proposes asymmetric perturbation, perturbing only one player's payoff function.

Reports that sufficiently small asymmetric perturbation preserves an equilibrium strategy of the original game and uses this result to construct a learning algorithm with a linear last-iterate convergence rate.
Provides a parameter-free variant that reportedly retains the linear rate.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper's stated distinction is to use one-sided rather than symmetric payoff perturbation, together with a parameter-free variant and linear-rate learning construction.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report equilibrium-strategy coincidence between the asymmetrically perturbed and original games when perturbation strength is sufficiently small.
The authors report that both the learning algorithm and its parameter-free variant have a linear last-iterate convergence rate.
The authors empirically demonstrate fast convergence toward equilibria in normal-form and extensive-form games.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames bilinear saddle-point optimization and introduces one-sided payoff perturbation.
Contrasts the proposal with symmetric perturbation, whose decreasing strength causes a slower rate.
States that sufficiently small asymmetric perturbation preserves an equilibrium strategy of the original game.
Builds a linear last-iterate learning algorithm and then gives a parameter-free variant retaining that rate.
Reports fast convergence toward equilibria in normal-form and extensive-form games.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a specific structural choice—perturbing only one player's payoff—to equilibrium preservation under a sufficiently small strength, then uses that link to motivate a linear-rate algorithm and a parameter-free variant.

lessons.interpretation: A method's design choice can serve as both the mechanism for a theoretical guarantee and the organizing rationale for later algorithmic extensions.
lessons.application: When presenting a new optimization method, explicitly connect its structural modification to the key theoretical property, then derive algorithmic variants from the property’s limiting condition.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the proposed modification has no stated mechanism or when its guarantee depends on conditions that cannot be specified or checked.

unknowns: The numerical meaning of “sufficiently small” perturbation strength is not given.
The assumptions, rate constants, and precise meaning of the parameter-free construction are unspecified.
The empirical protocols, baselines, and quantitative convergence results are not reported.
